This topic is genuinely useful beyond just Uber itself, since many companies structure their behavioral rounds around a specific, named list of values, and the general approach to preparing for this kind of round, researching the actual values and mapping stories to them, generalizes well across similar company structures.

blocks.content: 1. How a Culture Value Based Round Is Typically Structured
blocks.text: 1. How a Culture Value Based Round Is Typically Structured

blocks.content: A few real facts about this kind of round. It is built around a specific set of named company values, publicly documented by the company itself, similar in overall structure to the well known Amazon Leadership Principles system, though built around a genuinely different named list.

Questions and candidate stories are mapped against those specific named values, meaning the actual grading structure again rewards deliberately targeted stories over generic ones, much like the Amazon system covered earlier in this module.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784026078169-9585642.png
blocks.alt: A culture value based round is built around a specific, named set of company values, similar in structure to the Amazon Leadership Principles system

blocks.content: 2. Common Themes in This Kind of Round
blocks.text: 2. Common Themes in This Kind of Round

blocks.content: A few real themes tend to run through culture value based rounds at companies with an operationally intense, execution focused culture. Genuine ownership of outcomes, not just tasks, a real end to end sense of accountability for what actually happens, not just individual effort spent.

Real customer or user focused thinking, grounding decisions in actual end user impact rather than internal convenience alone. And a genuine bias toward building and shipping, actually getting something real into the world, rather than extended discussion or analysis without eventual action.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784026080028-747505281.png
blocks.alt: Common themes: genuine ownership of outcomes, real customer or user focused thinking, and a genuine bias toward building and shipping

3. A Worked Example

A concrete story shows this applied well. A solution was built and shipped quickly rather than over analyzed extensively, with genuine ownership taken for both the early misstep and the eventual, refined result.

First person quote: "I built and shipped a solution quickly rather than over analyzing it extensively beforehand. I owned the outcome fully, including a real early misstep that came from moving quickly, I did not shy away from naming that honestly. I kept the actual end user impact central throughout the process, checking real usage rather than just assuming the initial version was right. Once refined based on that real feedback, it delivered genuine, measurable value, a direct result of shipping fast and then owning the iteration that followed."
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784026081654-734815002.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: building and shipping quickly, owning a real early misstep honestly, keeping user impact central, and delivering measurable value once refined

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Telling a purely generic success story with no specific company value clearly reflected in it. A value based grading structure rewards stories deliberately mapped to specific named values, not generically strong stories alone.
4. A Generic Story Versus a Value Mapped Story
blocks.text: 4. A Generic Story Versus a Value Mapped Story

blocks.content: A generic story with no specific value in mind, while potentially a genuinely good story on its own merits, is a weaker fit for a value based grading structure, since it does not clearly demonstrate the specific named behaviors this kind of round is actually structured to evaluate.

A story deliberately chosen to reflect a specific named value, ownership, customer focus, bias for building, is a meaningfully stronger fit for this specific structure, since it directly hits the exact evaluation criteria the interviewer has been trained to grade against.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784026083303-825252511.png
blocks.alt: A generic story with no specific value in mind is a weaker fit for this structure; a story deliberately mapped to a specific named value is a meaningfully stronger fit

blocks.content: 5. Researching a Specific Company Actual Named Values
blocks.text: 5. Researching a Specific Company Actual Named Values

blocks.content: A few concrete steps genuinely help before this kind of interview. Reading the company own public description of its values directly, rather than assuming based on general industry reputation or secondhand summaries. Preparing at least one story that maps naturally to each major value, building a genuine bank similar to the approach covered for Amazon.

And avoiding the assumption that values are identical across different companies, even ones in similar industries, since specific named values, and their exact meaning within that company, genuinely differ from one company to the next.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784026085068-826811998.png
blocks.alt: Researching a company real values: read their own public description directly, prepare a story mapped to each major value, and avoid assuming values are identical across companies

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Assuming one company values are basically the same as another similar company values is a common, avoidable mistake. Reading the specific, named list directly is worth the small amount of time it takes.
6. Genuinely Common Failure Modes

A few real patterns undermine performance in this kind of round. Assuming a specific company values match another, similar company values exactly, rather than researching the actual, specific named list. Telling generic stories with no specific value clearly reflected, missing the deliberate mapping this structure rewards.
And describing ownership or bias for building only in the abstract, as a claimed personal trait, rather than through a real, specific, concrete story demonstrating it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784026086740-7008553.png
blocks.alt: Common failure modes: assuming values match another company, telling generic stories with no specific value reflected, and describing traits only in the abstract

blocks.content: 7. Preparing Your Own Value Based Interview Stories
blocks.text: 7. Preparing Your Own Value Based Interview Stories

blocks.content: Research the specific company own named values directly, then build a small bank of distinct stories, each deliberately mapped to one or more of those specific values, rather than relying on generic, unmapped stories.

The strongest preparation here mirrors the Amazon approach covered earlier in this module, recognize the underlying value being tested, then select the story from your bank that naturally demonstrates it.
A value based interview round rewards stories deliberately mapped to specific, named values, not generically good stories alone.
